title: Hypernatraemia (adult)
subject: nephrology
summary: Restore circulation first if shocked, then replace the free water deficit with enteral water or hypotonic IV fluid, lowering sodium by about 10 mmol/L per day in chronic cases and faster in acute salt loading, while treating the cause and ongoing losses.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Hypernatraemia: serum sodium above 145 mmol/L; cohort studies define severe as 155 mmol/L or more.
It reflects a water deficit relative to sodium, usually with impaired thirst or access to water: older adults, dementia, stroke, sedated or ventilated patients.

Causes: pure water loss (diabetes insipidus, fever, heat, tachypnoea), hypotonic fluid loss (diarrhoea, vomiting, osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia or mannitol, loop diuretics, lactulose, post-obstructive diuresis) or sodium gain (hypertonic saline, sodium bicarbonate, salt ingestion).
Features: thirst, lethargy, irritability, weakness, confusion, seizures and coma; brain shrinkage can cause intracranial haemorrhage.
Duration decides the safe rate: acute (developed over hours, for example accidental salt loading) versus chronic (over 48 hours or unknown).

sections.title: Initial assessment and calculation
items: Shock or poor perfusion: first restore circulation with a limited volume of isotonic crystalloid, then switch to hypotonic fluid once haemodynamically stable.
Total body water (TBW) = weight in kg x 0.6 in younger men, 0.5 in younger women and older men, 0.45 in older women.
Free water deficit (litres) = TBW x (serum sodium / 140 minus 1).
Expected change in serum sodium from 1 litre of infusate = (infusate sodium minus serum sodium) / (TBW + 1). Infusate sodium: 5% dextrose 0, 0.2% saline 34, 0.45% saline 77 mmol/L.
Set the rate from the formula to reach the daily target, then add maintenance needs and measured ongoing losses (urine, stool, drains).

sections.title: Fluids and correction rate
items: Route: oral or nasogastric water is preferred. If not feasible, give IV 5% dextrose for pure water loss, or 0.45% saline when sodium has also been lost (diarrhoea, osmotic diuresis).
Chronic or unknown duration: aim to lower sodium by about 10 mmol/L per day (classically no faster than 0.5 mmol/L/h) towards 145 mmol/L.
Acute hypernatraemia developing over hours: lowering by about 1 mmol/L/h is appropriate because brain adaptation has not occurred.

Adult cohort data (Feigin 2023, systematic review 2024) found no cerebral oedema attributable to correction faster than 0.5 mmol/L/h and higher mortality with slow correction: avoid under-treatment as well as overshoot.
Isotonic 0.9% saline is unsuitable for correcting hypernatraemia except for circulatory compromise.

sections.title: Treat the cause
items: Stop gastrointestinal losses, control fever and hyperglycaemia, and withhold lactulose and diuretics where possible.
Correct hypercalcaemia and hypokalaemia, which impair urine concentration.
Suspected central diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine, head injury or pituitary surgery): give water and seek endocrine advice on desmopressin.
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia): treat the cause and ensure free access to water.
Tube-fed or ICU patients: prescribe adequate free water with feeds and review hypertonic fluids and sodium-containing drugs.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Recheck sodium frequently (for example every 4 hours) during active IV correction and reassess the prescription each time.
Measure urine output and ongoing losses; a large dilute urine output suggests diabetes insipidus.
Check glucose when giving 5% dextrose: hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis and worsens hypernatraemia.
Watch for seizures or falling consciousness during treatment.

sections.title: Indian context
items: Heat stroke, diarrhoeal illness in older adults, and uncontrolled diabetes with osmotic diuresis are common precipitants in summer; check creatinine, glucose and CK.
Half-strength (0.45%) saline and 5% dextrose are widely available; 0.2% saline often is not, so use enteral water where the gut works.
Older adults with dementia, stroke or immobility need scheduled water intake, especially during heat waves and febrile illness.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Correcting with 0.9% saline in a stable patient, which worsens or fails to correct sodium.
Ignoring ongoing losses, so sodium does not fall as calculated.
Unduly slow correction in hospital-acquired hypernatraemia.
Missing hyperglycaemia or hypercalcaemia as the driver of polyuria.

drugs.name: Enteral water (oral or nasogastric)
drugs.dose: Volume from the free water deficit plus ongoing losses, spread to lower sodium about 10 mmol/L per day
drugs.notes: Preferred route when the gut works.

drugs.name: Glucose 5% IV
drugs.dose: Rate set by the Adrogue-Madias formula to lower sodium about 10 mmol/L per day (chronic) or 1 mmol/L/h (acute)

drugs.name: Sodium chloride 0.45% IV
drugs.dose: Rate set by the Adrogue-Madias formula
drugs.notes: When sodium has also been lost; a larger volume is needed than with 5% dextrose.

drugs.name: Isotonic crystalloid
drugs.dose: Limited IV boluses until perfusion is restored
drugs.notes: Shock only; then change to hypotonic fluid.
